concept.shortExplanation: Before anything is embedded, text is cut into tokens, and the model only ever sees those pieces. Byte-pair encoding builds its vocabulary greedily: start from single characters, then repeatedly merge whichever adjacent pair is most frequent in the training corpus, recording the order of those merges. At inference the same merges are replayed in the same order. This is why common English words are one token and unusual strings shatter into many — and why a model's cost, context limit and blind spots all trace back to this step.
concept.ahaMoment: The model never saw the word you typed. It saw a sequence of fragments chosen by frequency statistics in a corpus you have never read — and everything it 'knows' about your word is reconstructed from those pieces.

modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The GPT-2 tokenizer files could not be downloaded. Check your connection and retry — the tokenizer is only a few megabytes and works offline once cached.

levels.title: Count the Tokens
levels.instructions: Estimate how many tokens the real GPT-2 tokenizer produces for each string, then reveal. Watch what happens to rare words, whitespace and numbers.
hints: Common English words are usually one token each, but leading or repeated whitespace, digits and unusual symbols each tend to cost their own token — count words and count irregularities separately.

'The quick brown fox' is four ordinary words → four tokens. Long words built from familiar English prefixes and suffixes (like the parts of 'antidisestablishmentarianism') often tokenize into far fewer pieces than their letter count suggests, since GPT-2 has learned those parts as single tokens.
Real counts: 'The quick brown fox' = 4, 'antidisestablishmentarianism' = 5, '1234567890' = 4, the irregular-spacing string = 6, and the emoji line = 6.

levels.title: Merge Puzzle
levels.instructions: Start from single characters and apply byte-pair merges in the order the real tokenizer would. Each merge you pick is checked against GPT-2's actual merge ranks.
hints: Start from single characters and merge the pair that the real tokenizer would merge earliest — common two-letter combinations tend to merge before rarer ones, and the order is fixed by GPT-2's own training, not by what looks intuitive.
All three words end up as recognisable sub-word chunks — think about which prefix or suffix each word is built from that GPT-2 would already know as its own single token.
The final pieces are: 'lower' stays as one whole token (no split), 'newest' splits into 'new' + 'est', and 'tokenizer' splits into 'token' + 'izer'.

levels.title: Break the Tokenizer
levels.instructions: Free text. Find a string under 40 characters that produces the worst possible tokens-per-character ratio — the more tokens the tokenizer needs per character, the more badly it is coping.
hints: The tokenizer is efficient at English words it has seen often. It is inefficient at things it has almost never seen as a whole chunk — rare symbols, mixed scripts, and characters typed with no recognisable pattern.

Random keyboard mashing, uncommon Unicode characters (accented letters outside common European languages, symbols, emoji) and strings that mix scripts or alternate wildly in case tend to fragment into close to one token per character.

String together unusual symbols, emoji and rare accented or non-Latin characters with no repeating pattern — mixing several different kinds of 'unfamiliar' in one short string reliably drives the tokens-per-character ratio toward its worst case, since the tokenizer has almost no shared sub-word chunks to fall back on.
